analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from buying back their own stock and gives employees one-third of corporate board seats.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2023 with 33 House supporters, all Democrats, and was referred to the Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Reward Work Act would do two things. It would prohibit publicly traded companies from buying their own shares on the stock market (a 'buyback'), and it would require every company registering its shares with the Securities and Exchange Commission to let its employees elect one-third of the board of directors, in a one-worker-one-vote election. Companies would still be allowed to buy back stock through public tender offers, which involve making an offer directly to all shareholders rather than trading on an exchange. The bill was never considered by the committee or the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large public companies, who would gain elected seats on corporate boards and thus a formal voice in decisions like pay, layoffs, and buybacks. It could also benefit employees and communities if cash that companies now spend propping up their share price were redirected to wages, investment, or hiring — the stated rationale of the bill's supporters.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any company from purchasing its own shares on a national stock exchange, and repeals the SEC rule (Rule 10b-18) that currently gives companies a legal safe harbor to do so.

Requires that at least one-third of a company's board of directors be chosen by its own employees through a one-employee-one-vote election, as a condition of registering its securities, with the SEC and NLRB writing rules to make those elections fair and to reach that one-third within two years of enactment.

Still permits buybacks through tender offers — where a company makes a public offer directly to all shareholders — so a company can return cash to shareholders, but not through the quiet, day-to-day open-market purchases that critics say are timed to boost executive stock payouts.

analysis.who_pays: Large public companies and their executives, who lose the buyback tool that boosts earnings-per-share figures and stock-based compensation, and shareholders — including ordinary retirement savers with 401(k)s and index funds — if companies respond by paying out less cash to investors. Corporate boards would also cede one-third of their seats to employee representatives.

drawbacks.text: Economists disagree about how much buybacks actually hurt workers; some argue buybacks are an efficient way to return excess cash to investors, whose households include ordinary retirement savers holding index funds and 401(k)s, so a ban could reduce returns for those savers.

The buyback ban leaves a large loophole: companies can still repurchase shares through tender offers, which the bill expressly protects, so sophisticated companies could shift repurchases to that channel.

Requiring one-third employee-elected boards is a major restructuring of corporate governance that would apply to companies of all sizes at registration, and critics would argue it deters companies from listing shares in the U.S. and invites litigation over how employee elections are run.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core bet — that redirecting buyback cash toward workers and investment outweighs any loss to shareholders — is genuinely contested among economists, and the draft leaves a tender-offer loophole that a motivated company could exploit. But the employee board-seat provision is a concrete, structural change that would give workers a real voice rather than a disclosure, and the costs fall mainly on executives and large shareholders rather than on wages or consumer prices. The main practical weakness is that no independent analysis of the bill's economic effects is in the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a markup or vote on it before the Congress ended, so the full House never considered it.

narrative.text: Rep. Jesús 'Chuy' García of Illinois introduced the Reward Work Act on May 25, 2023, with 30 original cosponsors including Ro Khanna, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Katie Porter.
A total of 32 members cosponsored the bill; every one of them was a Democrat, and no Republican cosponsored.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no further step of any kind for the rest of the 118th Congress.
Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still sitting in committee, so it died without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large public companies, their executives, and major shareholders are better off: the buyback tool and all-stockholder boards survive untouched. The committee that declined to act faced no political cost, while the bill's supporters gained nothing beyond a cosponsorship record.

for.name: Rep. Jesús 'Chuy' García
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Reward Work Act banning open-market stock buybacks and requiring one-third employee-elected corporate boards.

for.name: House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: 32 cosponsors, including Ro Khanna, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Pramila Jayapal, and Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding their names in support; every cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for all securities legislation
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup, hearing vote, or floor recommendation on the bill after its referral; the bill sat untouched for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.role: Chair of the House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee's agenda and never scheduled the bill for consideration; supporters of a bill cannot force a markup without the chair's scheduling decision.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors plus the sponsor were Democrats, with no Republican support; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call to break down by party.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their boards
industries.note: They would lose the open-market buyback tool entirely and would have to seat one-third of their boards with employee-elected directors. Corporate boards currently decide buybacks and compensation without any worker representation, which is exactly what the bill would change.

Buybacks raise earnings-per-share and share prices, which directly increase the value of executive stock awards. Banning them on the open market removes the mechanism executives rely on to time payouts to their own stock grants.

Buybacks support the share prices of the stocks these funds hold, so a ban could trim returns; but some large shareholders also argue buybacks drain cash from productive investment. They had no formal role in the bill's fate.

industries.industry: Ordinary retirement savers (401(k) and index fund holders)
industries.note: They own shares through funds that benefit from buybacks, so a ban could reduce their investment returns in the short run; the bill's bet is that wage gains and redirected corporate investment would outweigh that over time.
